Load forecasting for regional integrated energy system based on 
complementary ensemble empirical mode decomposition and 
multi-model fusion 
Jian Shi , Jiashen Teh
* 
School of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, Universiti Sains Malaysia (USM), Nibong Tebal 14300, Penang, Malaysia   
HIGHLIGHTS 
• CEEMD technology reduces the complexity of data samples. 
• Multi-model fusion forecasting method improves the forecasting accuracy. 
• Sample entropy is used to extract the features of the Intrinsic Mode Function. 
• Parameter optimization using particle swarm optimization and genetic algorithm.

ABSTRACT  
The multiple loads of the Regional Integrated Energy System (RIES) possess characteristics of randomness and 
relatively higher complexity. The current forecasting methods struggle to effectively handle the non-stationary 
sequence of these multiple loads, leading to less accurate load forecasting. To address this problem, this paper 
proposes a multi-model fusion prediction method based on Complementary Ensemble Empirical Mode Decom -
position (CEEMD), Genetic Algorithm-Long Short Term Memory (GA-LSTM), Radial Basis Fusion-Autoencoder 
(RBF-AE), and Particle Swarm Optimization-Support Vector Machine (PSO-SVM). First, the load sequence is 
decomposed into different frequency Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) components using CEEMD. The IMFs 
components are then grouped based on their zero-crossing rate and Sample Entropy (SE), resulting in three 
distinct groups: high-, medium-, and low-frequency components. Next, the high-frequency load component, 
which exhibit strong randomness, are predicted using GA-LSTM. The medium-frequency load component, which 
have weaker randomness, are predicted using RBF-AE. The smooth and periodic low-frequency load component 
are predicted using PSO-SVM. The prediction results from these three models are reconstructed to obtain the final 
predictive value. Finally, experimental results confirm that the forecasting model can effectively handle non- 
stationary load sequences and demonstrate the highest level of forecasting accuracy.   
1. Introduction 
The primary objective of the Regional Integrated Energy System 
(RIES) is to improve the efficiency of various energy sources, including 
electric, cooling, heating, and others, by introducing greater diversity 
into the existing energy system. To ensure reliable and cost-effective 
operation of the RIES, precise load forecasting is essential. However, 
due to the interdependence among various loads, known as Coupled -
ness, within the RIES, a more sophisticated approach is required to 
forecast multi-element loads and meet the increased demands [ 1 ]. 
As the energy transition process gains momentum, the study of 
various types of load forecasting has witnessed a gradual surge. Methods 
like wavelet neural network, improved particle swarm, and attention- 
based convolutional neural network have been proposed in literature 
[ 2 – 4 ] to enhance the accuracy of load forecasting for integrated energy 
systems. Literature [ 5 ] presents a novel short-term load multi-step 
forecasting method based on long-and short-term time series network. 
On the other hand, literature [ 6 ] proposes a hybrid model called 
CEEMDAN-SE-TR, which incorporates Complete Ensemble Empirical 
Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN), SE, and

Optimization (LF-PSO) technique to optimize a deep learning model for 
load prediction. Meanwhile, literature [ 8 ] proposes a Bidirectional-Long 
Short Term Memory (BiLSTM) network for heat load prediction, and the 
Bi-LSTM model can improve the prediction accuracy of heat load in a 
district heating system by using both past and future weather informa -
tion. For short-term load prediction, literature [ 9 ] introduces a Kernel 
Extreme Learning Machine (KELM) based method, while literature [ 10 ] 
proposes a relatively simple artificial neural network-based model for 
short-term load forecasting, which can be used for single-category loads. 
The aforementioned prediction methods are relatively simple, as they 
are all based on a single prediction model, which is suitable for handling 
a single type of load. Furthermore, when confronted with highly fluc -
tuating loads, the predictive capability is inadequate. And these models 
lack the ability to handle high-dimensional feature vectors. In RIES 
where electric, cooling and heating loads are interdependent, more 
complex forecasting models are required to improve accuracy in 
forecasting. 
Predicting raw data directly leads to significant errors. Over the past 
few years, researchers have introduced signal decomposition techniques 
to construct advanced deep learning prediction models. The study in 
[ 11 ] proposed a novel hybrid prediction model, which combines Com -
plementary Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition (CEEMD), Sample 
Entropy (SE), Random Forest (RF), Improved Reptile Search Algorithm 
(IRSA), Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) and BiLSTM. Firstly, the 
CEEMD technique is applied to break down the initial sequence into a set 
of more stable components. Secondly, SE segregates these components 
into high and low-frequency components. The RF algorithm is employed 
to eliminate redundant features, and BiLSTM and ELM are employed to 
predict the high and low-frequency components, respectively. The out -
comes indicate that the hybrid prediction model exhibits robust pre -
dictive capabilities. The Bidirectional Gated Recursive Unit (BiGRU) 
demonstrates robust capabilities in nonlinear fitting and effective 
mapping for prediction. The study in [ 12 ] proposed a prediction 
approach referred to as VMD-CNN-BiGRU. In this approach, the first step 
involves applying Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) to break 
down the original sequence. Secondly, Convolutional Neural Networks 
(CNN) are employed to uncover potential input-output relationship, 
extracting significant feature correlations. Lastly, prediction is accom -
plished using Bidirectional Gated Recursive Units (BiGRU). The out -
comes indicate that this model exhibits high prediction accuracy. 
The load forecasting for RIES proposed in this paper faces challenges 
in meeting the constantly fluctuating demands of residents and busi -
nesses, which makes accurate predictions more difficult. To tackle this 
issue, literature [ 13 ] suggests an integrated load forecasting model 
based on Bidirectional Generative Adversarial Networks, while litera -
ture [ 14 ] proposes a short-term multi-energy load forecasting method 
using a predictive model for multi-task learning. Other studies, such as 
literature [ 15 – 17 ], propose prediction models based on least squares 
support vector machine, long short memory neural network model, 
CNN, and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU). The aforementioned forecasting 
model disregards the significant non-stationary characteristics of 
multivariate loads and lacks comprehensive load processing. Conse -
quently, it directly predicts the loads, resulting in low accuracy. 
Generally speaking, the model ’ s applicability is limited, and it tends to 
produce prediction errors when faced with challenging data. 
Adequate raw data preprocessing is essential for load forecasting, as 
it has a direct impact on the model ’ s performance and its ability to 
provide accurate predictions. Signal decomposition techniques can 
assume a pivotal role in predictive data processing, particularly when 
handling intricate load data featuring complex structures and multi- 
scale components. The study in [ 18 ] proposed a prediction model 
named Time Varying Filtering based Empirical Mode Decomposition- 
Partial Autocorrelation Function-Improved Chimp Optimization 
Algorithm-Bidirectional Gated Recurrent Unit (TVFEMD-PACF-IChOA- 
BiGRU) is introduced. This model employs TVFEMD to decompose the 
initial wind speed data. TVFEMD is an adaptive method well-suited for 
handling nonlinear and non-stationary signals. Experimental results 
prove that this method inherits the advantages of high frequency sepa -
ration performance and stability at low sampling rates, and has strong 
immunity to noise interference and robustness to wind speed data pro -
cessing. Furthermore, IChOA is applied to refine the weight coefficients, 
resulting in improved prediction accuracy. The study in [ 19 ] proposed a 
model called Variational Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Regression 
(VHGPR). This model is designed with the aim of delivering robust and 
broadly applicable predictions for wind speed, showcasing high- 
performance characteristics. The CEEMDAN technique is employed for 
preprocessing the initial dataset. CEEMDAN effectively addresses mode 
mixing issues in empirical mode decomposition, exhibits minimal noise 
interference, and proves suitable for handling intricate nonlinear and 
non-stationary signals. Empirical findings demonstrate that integrating 
the CEEMDAN decomposition approach with this prediction model 
yields enhanced predictive accuracy. 
In order to improve the forecasting accuracy, literature [ 20 ] employs 
VMD to decompose the wind speed sequence into various eigenmode 
components, which are then utilized by the Long Short Term Memory 
(LSTM)neural network for prediction. However, VMD is only suitable for 
processing signals with highly concentrated frequencies in a short period 
of time, which can be attributed to external shocks and natural factors 
that may affect the power grid. In the case of RIES, the long-term fluc -
tuations of the overall data need to be taken into account, which makes 
the Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) method more appropriate. 
The EMD process involves screening the original load data by identi -
fying all extreme points of the signal, including the maximum and 
minimum values, and then taking the average of these points to create a 
line. This line is then subtracted from the original signal, resulting in a 
sieving process. The EMD process separates the original signal into 
different frequency components, and then filters each component to the 
last remaining monotonic function line. In simpler terms, EMD can be 
compared to a machine that separates a bunch of mixed coins into 
several parts based on their value, such as 10 dollars, 1 dollar, 5 cents, 
and 1 cent. In literature [ 21 ], EMD is used. Although each component is 
consistent with the original sequence after reconstruction, EMD exhibits 
a modal mixing phenomenon, where the decomposed high-frequency 
components are non-stationary components. Predicting these compo -
nents may result in a error. To reduce the impact of non-stationary 
components generated by decomposition on prediction, Literature 
[ 22 ] employs a set EMD to decompose the component again. However, 
this approach introduces noise, and the second decomposition generates 
too many components, making the forecasting process very time- 
consuming. Therefore, the EMD method suffers from some drawbacks 
such as modal aliasing and low efficiency, which ultimately leads to low 
prediction accuracy. Given the aforementioned issues with EMD, this 
paper proposes the use of the CEEMD method to decompose the original 
load. Unlike the EMD method that adds a set of white noise to each 
decomposition, the CEEMD adds a set of positive and negative white 
noise. This approach can offset the noisy data during decomposition in

CEEMD is a method for EMD that adjusts the amplitude locally. It 
involves breaking down the original signal into various IMFs and a re -
sidual term. The front IMFs typically contain high-frequency compo -
nents, the middle IMFs contain medium-frequency components, and the 
latter IMFs and RES contain low-frequency components. The same pre -
diction model is used for all the IMFs components obtained via CEEMD 
decomposition, and the predictions are combined by superimposition to 
obtain the final prediction value. However, the prediction accuracy 
achieved by this method is not ideal, particularly when it comes to RIES 
multi-element load prediction. In the literature [20], LSTM is employed 
to predict all the IMFs obtained by decomposition. However, LSTM 
shows poor prediction performance and takes a long time to process low- 
frequency components [25]. This paper proposes a method to group the 
IMFs components obtained through CEEMD decomposition and select a 
suitable sub-prediction model for each group. To improve the effec -
tiveness of grouping, the paper introduces the use of zero-crossing rate 
and SE as grouping criteria. The zero-crossing rate is a measure of the 
number of times a signal crosses the zero point in a given time period 
[23]. In signal processing, it is often used to quantify the number of zero- 
crossing points in an audio or vibration signal. A zero crossing occurs 
when the signal changes polarity from positive to negative, or vice versa. 
By analyzing the zero-crossing rate of a signal, it is possible to distin -
guish between the high-, medium-, and low-frequency components. 
Generally, low-frequency components have lower zero-crossing rates 
because they change more slowly. Medium-frequency components 
usually have moderate zero-crossing rates, while high-frequency com -
ponents have high zero-crossing rates because they change rapidly. The 
interdependent relationship among the three subsystems of electric, 
cooling and heating in RIES is complex. Therefore, signal analysis may 
encounter more noise and nonlinearity, making it necessary to consider 
the SE of each component for effective analysis and distinguishing be -
tween high-, medium-, and low frequency components. SE is a technique 
for assessing the complexity of a time series. It can be used to identify the 
nonlinear components in the signal sequence based on their complexity. 
Typically, high-frequency components contain more nonlinear compo -
nents, while low-frequency components contain fewer nonlinear com -
ponents [24]. To more accurately differentiate between the high-, 
medium-, and low-frequency components obtained by CEEMD decom -
position, this paper incorporates both the zero-crossing rate and SE. 
This paper undertakes a comprehensive examination utilizing the 
RIES as a framework. It involves breaking down the data on electric, 
cooling and heating loads within the system, leading to the identifica -
tion of high-frequency, medium-frequency, and low-frequency compo -
nents. The high-frequency component embodies the swift variations and 
immediate fluctuations observed in the electric cooling and heating load 
data. It mirrors the short-term shifts in demand and showcases the sys -
tem’s ability to respond promptly to these changes. High-frequency 
components encompass instantaneous power demand fluctuations, as 
well as rapid changes in cooling and heating loads. They capture tran -
sient responses, unexpected events, and both internal and external dis -
turbances affecting the system. These components wield significant 
influence over the flexibility and stability of system operations. The 
medium-frequency component pertains to the medium-term alterations 
and periodic fluctuations observed in the electric cooling and heating 
load data. It signifies the seasonal, periodic, and repetitive changes in 
the load. Medium-frequency components encompass seasonal variations 
in electricity, cooling, and heating loads, as well as cyclical patterns and 
distinctions between working and non-working days. They bear signif -
icant implications for system planning, scheduling, and resource allo -
cation. The low-frequency component captures the long-term trends and 
gradual patterns in the electric cooling and heating load data. It reflects 
the impacts of long-term economic development, population growth, 
and structural changes in the load, among other factors. Low-frequency 
components encompass long-term trends, annual variations, economic 
cycles, and more in electricity, cooling, and heating loads. They play a 
crucial role in system planning, long-term energy demand forecasting, 
investment decision-making, and policy development. 
This paper chooses the suitable forecasting model to predict the IMFs 
of three distinct frequencies. In accordance with literature [25], a load 
forecasting method is proposed that combines the multiple linear 
regression forecasting method and LSTM. This method dissects the load 
sequence into different frequency components and employs LSTM to 
predict high-frequency components that exhibit strong randomness. The 
outcomes indicate a higher level of prediction accuracy. LSTM is a 
neural network that is well suited for time series data due to its long- 
term memory unit, which can capture long-term dependencies in 
sequential data. It is appropriate for handling high-frequency data with 
time series characteristics. High-frequency data often exhibit temporal 
correlations, and LSTM is a suitable model for processing and predicting 
such data. Given the strong time series characteristics present in the 
RIES multivariate load data, the decision has been made in this paper to 
utilize LSTM for the prediction of high-frequency components. 
A prediction method incorporating variational mode decomposition- 
wavelet transform and principal component analysis-backpropagation 
screening-radial basis function was proposed in the literature [26]. By 
decomposing and denoising the raw data sequence, the method aims to 
extract a medium-frequency component that exhibits relative stability. 
This extracted component is subsequently fed into a Radial Basis 
Function (RBF) neural network for prediction purposes. Notably, the 
final prediction results obtained through this approach demonstrate a 
high level of accuracy. The RBF neural network is a nonlinear model that 
employs radial basis functions to determine the weighting of its output. 
It is particularly effective in high-dimensional spaces. In the context of 
RIES multivariate load forecasting, the interdependence between elec -
tric, cooling, heating loads and meteorological factors plays a vital role 
in predicting multivariate loads. Understanding and incorporating the 
coupling characteristics among these factors are crucial for accurate 
multivariate load forecasting in the RIES framework. In order to make 
accurate predictions, predictive models necessitate the use of high- 
dimensional feature vectors. Consequently, RBF neural network is the 
best choice to predicting medium-frequency components. 
The time series forecasting model described in literature [27] com -
bines the Wavelet Neural Network (WNN) and Support Vector Machine 
(SVM) techniques to improve predictions. The process begins by 
applying wavelet decomposition to a time series, separating it into high- 
and low-frequency components. The high-frequency components are 
fitted using a WNN model, while a SVM model is employed to predict the 
low-frequency components. The sub-model’s predicted value is subse -
quently reconstructed, resulting in a highly accurate final prediction. 
The literature indicates that SVM demonstrates remarkable generaliza -
tion ability and robustness when it comes to predicting low-frequency 
components. The IMF obtained through RIES multivariate load decom -
position often contains numerous outliers and noise, and SVM is adept at 
mitigating the impact of these factors on prediction outcomes. Conse -
quently, this paper employs SVM for the prediction of low-frequency 
components. 
This paper proposes CEEMD and Multi-model Fusion (CEEMD-MF) 
prediction methods. The main contributions of this paper are:  
(i) The distinctive features exhibited by RIES multiple loads, 
particularly their significant fluctuations, are explored in this 
paper by drawing from the background of RIES. A novel data 
processing technique called frequency grouping is introduced, 
which is specifically tailored to address these characteristics. The 
proposed method focuses on a sequence of non-stationary IMFs 
and effectively partitions them into three distinct frequency 
components by combining SE and zero-crossing rate. Multi-scale 
features in load data are enhanced, noise is eliminated, and the 
precision and dependability of predictions are enhanced through 
the use of this method.

The paper is structured as follows: The framework of CEEMD-MF is 
outlined in Section II, and its forecasting method is introduced. 
Furthermore, GA-LSTM, PSO-SVM, RBF-AE, CEEMD, and SE are pre -
sented. In Section III, the data is processed and decomposed, and the 
resulting IMF components are categorized as high-, medium-, and low- 
frequency. The simulation experiment is then conducted from four 
different perspectives. Firstly, the impact of CEEMD on accuracy is 
evaluated by comparing it with LSTM, GA-LSTM, RBF-AE, and PSO- 
SVM. Secondly, the advantages of CEEMD are analyzed and compared 
with EEMD-MF and VMD-MF. The third point involves analyzing the 
impact of multi-model fusion on accuracy. This is done by comparing it

to assess the reliability of the model, a comparison is made with ELM, 
BPNN, GRU, TCN, ISSA-LSSVM, and CEEMD-SSA-LSSVM. The conclu -
sion is provided in Section IV.

nology, Zero-crossing rates, SE, GA-LSTM, PSO-SVM, and RBF-AE to

2.1. Data processing 
Data preprocessing is necessary for load forecasting. The following 
are the processing steps:  
(i) Data cleaning: In the initial step of data cleaning, the original 
dataset is thoroughly processed to eliminate any potential errors, 
anomalies, or missing data. This process may involve handling 
missing values, addressing duplicate entries, and correcting 
erroneous data, among other tasks. By doing so, the data is 
refined and prepared for further analysis or modeling. Specif -
ically, this phase involves three major steps. 1) The process of 
handling missing values involves utilizing the imputation method 
to replace any missing values, specifically by selecting the mean 
value for imputation. 2) Outlier handling, Outlier handling in -
volves dealing with data points that exhibit notable deviations 
from the rest of the observations. In this paper, statistical tech -
niques are applied to identify outliers, and subsequent correc -
tions are made to address them. 3) Standardizing Units: The 
electric, cooling and heating data sets contain inconsistent units, 
which are then harmonized to a uniform unit of KW/h. This 
standardization guarantees data consistency and facilitates 
effective data comparisons.  
(ii) Data normalization: In order to ensure consistent predictions and 
avoid the disproportionate influence of various features, it is 
necessary to normalize the input data prior to making 
predictions.

2.2. Load forecasting evaluation index

2.8. Considerations for distinct prediction methods 
This paper employs distinct prediction techniques for high-, medium- 
and low-frequency, taking into account the following factors:  
(i) Different time scales consideration: The high-, medium-, and low- 
frequency components represent variations in the load data 
across different time scales. High-frequency components capture 
short-term fluctuations and rapid changes, medium-frequency 
components correspond to medium-term periodic changes, 
while low-frequency components capture long-term trends and 
gradual changes. Since these components exhibit distinct tem -
poral characteristics, employing different forecasting methods 
can effectively accommodate their specific patterns of change. 
(ii) Consideration of different influencing factors: The high-, me -
dium-, and low-frequency components can be influenced by 
distinct factors. High-frequency components are typically influ -
enced by instantaneous factors and noise, medium-frequency 
components are influenced by seasonal factors and cyclical 
changes, while low-frequency components are affected by long- 
term trends and structural factors. Employing different predic -
tion methods can effectively capture the characteristics and 
changing patterns of these components in relation to their 
respective influencing factors. 
(iii) Consideration of the predictive model ’ s fitness: Different fore -
casting methods exhibit varying adaptability and effectiveness in 
handling data with different time scales and changing patterns. In 
the case of studying the regional integrated energy system, the 
high-frequency components representing short-term fluctuations, 
as decomposed within this system, are better suited for utilization 
of time series-based models. This paper specifically employs the 
LSTM neural network, which aligns well with capturing and 
predicting the dynamics of these high-frequency components. 
The intermediate frequency components, characterized by peri -
odic changes and their association with electric, cooling and 
heating, require the input of high-dimensional feature vectors. 
These components are better suited for seasonal models. In this 
paper, the RBF model is chosen as it excels in handling high- 
dimensional feature vectors. The RBF model leverages its own 
function approximation capabilities to effectively capture 
nonlinear relationships within seasonal data. The low-frequency 
component typically represents the long-term trend and slow 
changes in the load data. In this paper, the SVM model is chosen 
to forecast this component. As a nonlinear classification and 
regression method, SVM exhibits robust noise suppression capa -
bilities and demonstrates good prediction performance. By 
selecting an appropriate forecasting method like SVM, the char -
acteristics and parameters of the model can be effectively lever -
aged to enhance the accuracy of load forecasting.  
(iv) Distinguishing data characteristics: The high-, medium-, and low- 
frequency components exhibit distinct characteristics in terms of 
frequency domain, amplitude, fluctuation ranges, and variation 
ranges. By employing different prediction methods, these unique 
features can be effectively captured, enabling more accurate 
predictions of the behavior and patterns exhibited by each 
component.

The paper conducts simulation experiments from various perspec -
tives, and the results confirm the effectiveness and high accuracy of the 
CEEMD-MF prediction model. Based on the information presented in the 
tables and figures, the following discussions can be drawn:  
(i) The conclusion can be drawn that the prediction accuracy of 
models that do not use CEEMD for load decomposition is 
relatively poor. Based on the prediction results of different 
models, the CEEMD-MF proposed in this paper has the highest 
accuracy.  
(ii) Sub-prediction models demonstrated further improvement in 
prediction performance after undergoing hyperparameter opti -
mization or model fusion dimensionality reduction processing. 
Specifically, these models displayed higher prediction accuracy 
in processing the corresponding frequency components.

(iii) The multi-model fusion prediction method proves effective in 
handling non-stationary components obtained through CEEMD 
decomposition. The three sub-prediction models predict high-, 
medium-, and low frequency, which are then reconstructed to 
obtain the final prediction value. Comparative analysis results 
demonstrate that the CEEMD-MF model has the highest predic -
tion accuracy and the smallest error. 
Because RIES multivariate loads exhibit significant randomness and 
volatility, direct prediction leads to substantial errors. Thus, employing 
CEEMD to decompose the initial loads is essential for accurate fore -
casting. The decomposition results in a series of IMFs with different 
frequencies. In order to predict the IMFs with different frequencies 
effectively, it is necessary to select an appropriate prediction model for 
each component. To achieve this, the IMFs are categorized into high-, 
medium-, and low-frequency components by evaluating their zero- 
crossing rate and sample entropy. This division enables the identifica -
tion of the most suitable prediction model for each specific frequency 
component. For the high-frequency components, LSTM is chosen as the 
preferred prediction model. LSTM units excel at capturing long-term 
dependencies in sequential data, making them well-suited for handling 
high-frequency data that exhibit time series characteristics. The 
medium-frequency component is predicted using the RBF, which is 
known for its strong performance in high-dimensional spaces. In RIES 
multivariate load forecasting, accurate predictions rely on using high- 
dimensional feature vectors as input for forecasting. This makes RBF 
neural networks an excellent choice for modeling and forecasting. SVM 
is selected for low-frequency components. SVM demonstrates good 
generalization ability and robustness in predicting low-frequency com -
ponents. The RIES multivariate load sequence often contains outliers 
and noise, and SVM can effectively mitigate the impact of such noise and 
outliers on the prediction results. After undergoing hyperparameter 
optimization and model fusion, the three selected models were utilized 
for processing specific frequency components. Finally, the prediction 
results of these sub-models were reconstructed to obtain the final fore -
cast value. Following a thorough comparative analysis, the multi-model 
fusion approach demonstrated higher prediction accuracy. 
4. Conclusions 
To address the challenge of forecasting RIES multivariate loads with 
high volatility and randomness, this study proposes a load forecasting 
approach that uses CEEMD and multi-model fusion. The conclusions are 
as follows:  
(i) In this paper, a novel data processing method is proposed, which 
combines the CEEMD frequency division technique with SE and 
zero-crossing rate. This method effectively addresses the chal -
lenge of predicting data with high volatility and instability, 
leading to a notable improvement in prediction accuracy. When 
compared to the prediction method that does not utilize modal 
decomposition, the CEEMD-MF approach demonstrates a reduc -
tion in MAPE for electric, cooling and heating by 1.85 – 4.12%, 
2.49 – 3.08%, and 1.8 – 2.8%. 
(ii) To assess the efficacy and advantages of CEEMD, this study in -
corporates EEMD and VMD decompositions, comparing CEEMD- 
MF with EEMD-MF and VMD-MF. The results table shows that 
CEEMD-MF outperforms the other two decomposition prediction 
methods in terms of MAPE for electric load, cooling load, and 
heating load, exhibiting reductions of 2.64 – 3.13%, 0.55 – 1.94%, 
and 1.94 – 2.43% respectively.  
(iii) In this paper, a combined forecasting approach is employed, 
wherein different frequency components are selected and paired 
with suitable models. The resulting MAPE for electric ， cooling 
and heating load is observed to be 0.84 – 2.32%, 0.5 – 1.8%, and 
1.15 – 2.27% lower than the MAPE of the single load forecasting 
method following modal decomposition.  
(iv) The effectiveness of the proposed CEEMD-MF multivariate load 
forecasting method is demonstrated through a comparison with 
various other forecasting models including BPNN, ELM, TCN, 
GRU, ISSA-LSSVM, and CEEMD-SSA-LSSVM. The results indicate 
that the CEEMD-MF method consistently outperforms these 
models, resulting in a reduction in MAPE for electric cooling and 
heating by 0.73 – 3.8%, 0.42 – 3.6%, and 0.56 – 4.45%, respectively.
